opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I'd really love to see by the end of 2025 is that we cross a threshold where designing an antibody becomes more of an engineering problem than a discovery problem. Right now, the way most antibodies get made is still remarkably empirical. You immunize an animal, or you screen enormous libraries, and then you spend months doing affinity maturation and developability optimization, hoping something sticks. It works, but it's slow and expensive, and it fundamentally limits which targets people are willing to go after.

So my hope is that AI-driven design gets good enough that you can specify a target, a specific epitope even, and get back binders that actually work in the lab with a meaningful hit rate. Not one in ten thousand, but something like one in ten, or better. And ideally zero-shot, without needing rounds and rounds of experimental iteration to rescue the designs.

If we get there, it changes the economics of the whole field. You could go after epitopes that are hard to hit with traditional methods, like conserved regions on viral proteins, or tricky GPCRs and ion channels. You could design for developability properties from the start rather than fixing them afterwards. And you could imagine a world where a small team can generate high-quality therapeutic candidates in weeks instead of years.

I'd also say it's important to be honest that we're not fully there yet. The models are getting impressively good at structure, but function, specificity, immunogenicity, manufacturability, those are harder to capture. So part of what I hope 2025 brings is tighter loops between the computational side and high-throughput wet lab experiments, so the models are learning from real biological data at scale. That's the flywheel that I think ultimately makes this work.

r001.rationale: It expresses hope for AI antibody design by the end of 2025, but does not specify full-length IgG antibodies.

r002.rationale: It hopes to produce working binders with a meaningful hit rate, but does not mention designing CDR regions or say that doing so produces strong target binding.

r003.rationale: It mentions specifying a target or epitope and hopes for zero-shot design, but does not describe selecting a surface on an enzyme and binding it in a single attempt.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're in the middle of a transition from "can a model propose a binder at all" to "can a model propose binders reliably enough that you'd stake a program on it." Those are very different bars.

What I'd love to see by the end of the year is a real shift in hit rates. Historically, if you ran a de novo design campaign against a new target, you might screen thousands of candidates and be thrilled with a handful that bind at all, usually weakly. The interesting question is whether generative models can compress that funnel, so that a small set of designs gets you something with genuine affinity and specificity. That's less about any single heroic design and more about whether the process becomes boring and repeatable.

The second thing is harder targets. Antibodies have mostly worked well against accessible, well-behaved surfaces. The targets people actually care about clinically are often conformationally dynamic, or membrane-embedded, or you need to hit a specific state of the protein rather than the protein in general. Epitope-specific design, where you say "bind here, not there," is where I think models could be genuinely differentiating, because that's exactly what immunization and display libraries are bad at controlling.

Third, and this is the part I think gets underrated, the developability properties. A tight binder that aggregates, or has terrible expression, or triggers immunogenicity, isn't a drug. Some of those properties are much easier to learn from data than binding is, because there are large internal datasets at every antibody company. I'd be happy if we got to the point where you're co-optimizing affinity and manufacturability in the same loop instead of discovering problems eighteen months later.

Underneath all of it is a data problem. Structure prediction got where it is because of decades of crystallography deposited in a public database. We don't have the equivalent for antibody-antigen binding measured quantitatively at scale. Most of that data is proprietary, inconsistently measured, and heavily biased toward things that worked. So a lot of the near-term progress probably comes from labs building purpose-made measurement datasets, with the explicit goal of training on them, rather than from scraping what already exists.

So my realistic hope isn't a fully computational antibody in the clinic by December. It's that a few groups show, convincingly and reproducibly, that the computational path has a better hit rate than the experimental one on targets that matter. Once that's established, the field reorganizes around it pretty quickly.

r001.rationale: The response hopes for better, reproducible hit rates, but does not say AI will design full-length IgG antibodies by the end of 2025. It explicitly says a fully computational antibody in the clinic by December is not its realistic hope.

r002.rationale: The response discusses generative models producing binders with affinity, but does not mention designing CDR regions or state that doing so produces strong target binding.

r003.rationale: The response describes epitope-specific design as binding “here, not there,” but does not describe selecting a surface on an enzyme or achieving that design in a single attempt.

astra-6.text:
My hope is that we can go from specifying a target to having an antibody with the properties we want much more reliably. Not just something that binds, but something that’s specific, stable, and has a plausible path toward becoming a medicine.

By the end of 2025, I’d love to see compelling prospective demonstrations: design antibodies against difficult targets, make them, and show experimentally that they work. The exciting possibility is a much faster loop between computational design and biological testing, so we can explore therapeutic ideas that would otherwise be too expensive or too slow to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response hopes for reliable antibody design and experimental demonstrations by 2025, but does not specify full-length IgG antibodies.

r002.rationale: It mentions antibodies that bind, but does not say that designing CDR regions can produce strong target binding.

r003.rationale: It does not describe selecting a surface on an enzyme or achieving that binding in a single attempt.

sol-6.1.text: My hope is that we can move from finding antibodies largely through screening to designing them with much more control. You’d specify the target, where you want the antibody to bind, and the properties it needs, and get candidates that work when you test them in the lab. By the end of 2025, I’d be excited to see convincing demonstrations of that across multiple targets. That wouldn’t mean we’ve solved drug development, but it could make the first step toward a new therapy much faster and open up targets that have been difficult to approach.

r001.rationale: It hopes for more controlled antibody design and candidates that work, but does not specify full-length IgG antibodies.

r002.rationale: It does not mention CDR regions or state that designing them can produce strong target binding.

r003.rationale: It refers to choosing where an antibody should bind, but does not specify an enzyme surface or a successful single attempt.
